items.stem: Giedd et al. (1999) found that grey matter in the frontal lobes:
options: Increased until around puberty and then declined
Only increased after age 25
Remained constant throughout adolescence
Decreased steadily from birth
items.answer: Increased until around puberty and then declined
items.markingKey: A. Frontal grey matter peaked at about 11 in girls and 12 in boys, consistent with synaptic pruning afterwards.

items.stem: Aiko writes: "The adolescent brain is simply an immature adult brain." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Adolescence is a distinct period of reorganisation with heightened reward sensitivity and plasticity, which supports learning and social development as well as risk.
items.markingKey: Adolescence is a distinct period of reorganisation with heightened reward sensitivity and plasticity, which supports learning and social development as well as risk. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between white matter development and grey matter development.
items.answer: Grey matter increases in childhood and then decreases through pruning in adolescence, while white matter increases steadily through myelination into adulthood.
items.markingKey: Grey matter increases in childhood and then decreases through pruning in adolescence, while white matter increases steadily through myelination into adulthood. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Describe the study by Gardner and Steinberg (2005) and explain what it shows about the role of peers and the developing brain in adolescent risk-taking.
items.answer: Gardner and Steinberg (2005). Aim: to investigate whether the presence of peers increases risk-taking more in adolescents than in adults. Method: 306 participants in three age groups (13-16, 18-22, 24 and over) played a video driving game ("Chicken") alone or with two friends present, and completed risk questionnaires. Findings: peers doubled risky driving in adolescents, increased it by about half in young adults and had no significant effect in adults Link: the role of peers and the developing brain in adolescent risk-taking.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for accurate description of the study (aim, method, findings: peers doubled risky driving in adolescents, increased it by about half in young adults and had no significant effect in adults); up to 2 marks for explicitly linking the findings to the role of peers and the developing brain in adolescent risk-taking. items.stem: Using Gogtay et al. (2004) as supporting evidence, explain the late maturation of the prefrontal cortex.
items.answer: Gogtay et al. (2004). Aim: to map the sequence in which grey matter matures across the cortex. Method: 13 healthy children were scanned with MRI every two years for 8-10 years, starting at age 4-8, and cortical grey matter density was mapped over time. Findings: grey matter loss proceeded from back to front: sensory and motor areas matured first and the prefrontal cortex last Link: the late maturation of the prefrontal cortex.

items.stem: Critically assess the view that adolescent behaviour can be explained by brain development. Consider at least one methodological and one ethical or cultural issue.
items.answer: Brain development contributes to adolescent behaviour but interacts with social and cultural context; it is not a complete explanation.

items.stem: Describe the study by Piaget (1952) and explain what it shows about stages of cognitive development.
items.answer: Piaget (1952). Aim: to investigate when children understand that number stays the same despite changes in arrangement. items.stem: Describe the study by McGarrigle and Donaldson (1974) and explain what it shows about whether Piaget underestimated children's abilities.
items.answer: McGarrigle and Donaldson (1974). Aim: to test whether children's failure on conservation tasks was due to the way the task was presented. Method: 80 Scottish children aged 4-6 did number conservation tasks in which either the experimenter deliberately rearranged the counters or a "naughty teddy" messed them up "accidentally". Findings: about 62% conserved number in the naughty teddy condition compared with 16% when the experimenter changed the row Link: whether Piaget underestimated children's abilities.

items.stem: Distinguish between accommodation and assimilation.
items.answer: Assimilation fits new information into an existing schema (calling a zebra a "horse"); accommodation changes the schema to fit new information (creating a "zebra" schema).

items.stem: A teacher in Nairobi notices that 5-year-olds think a tall, thin glass holds more juice than a short, wide one. Using Piaget's theory, explain this and suggest how the teacher could help.
items.answer: Preoperational children show centration (focusing on height) and lack reversibility, so they fail conservation; hands-on pouring activities create disequilibrium and support accommodation; Vygotskian guided questioning can also help.

items.stem: With reference to teenage drivers and passengers, explain how it illustrates adolescent brain development.

items.stem: With reference to Wood, Bruner and Ross (1976), explain how research has investigated scaffolding in the zone of proximal development.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Piaget's theory provides an accurate account of cognitive development."
items.answer: Piaget described major changes in thinking but underestimated young children and the role of culture and social interaction.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: conservation and stages widely replicated in Western samples; influential in education (discovery learning). Arguments against: underestimated children (McGarrigle and Donaldson, 1974; Baillargeon and DeVos, 1991); underestimated social and cultural influences (Vygotsky); stages are less fixed than proposed. Supported judgement: Piaget described major changes in thinking but underestimated young children and the role of culture and social interaction.

items.stem: Critically assess the view that gender roles are mainly the result of sociocultural factors. Consider at least one methodological and one ethical or cultural issue.
items.answer: Gender roles are strongly shaped by sociocultural factors, interacting with biological predispositions.

items.stem: Harlow (1958) found that infant rhesus monkeys spent most time with:

items.stem: Using Baillargeon and DeVos (1991) as supporting evidence, explain early object permanence in infancy.
items.answer: Baillargeon and DeVos (1991). Aim: to investigate whether infants younger than Piaget proposed understand object permanence. Method: Infants aged about 3.5 months watched a short or tall carrot pass behind a screen with a window; in the impossible event the tall carrot did not appear in the window. Looking time was measured. Findings: infants looked longer at the impossible event, suggesting they expected the tall carrot to remain visible and understood it continued to exist behind the screen Link: early object permanence in infancy.
